question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 5-year history of perennial nasal symptoms — bilateral congestion, postnasal drip, and occasional watery rhinorrhoea — triggered by cold air, strong perfumes, and changes in humidity. Skin-prick testing and serum specific IgE are negative. Which diagnosis best fits?

answers.text: Perennial allergic rhinitis due to house dust mite sensitisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Perennial allergic rhinitis is driven by specific IgE to perennial allergens (dust mite, cockroach, mould). The negative skin-prick test and serum IgE exclude an IgE-mediated mechanism, ruling out allergic rhinitis.

Correct. Vasomotor rhinitis is diagnosed when perennial nasal symptoms are driven by non-specific physical and chemical triggers (cold air, smoke, perfume, humidity) in the absence of allergy (negative IgE testing) and infection. Autonomic dysregulation of the nasal vasculature is the underlying mechanism.

Incorrect. Atrophic rhinitis is characterised by progressive mucosal atrophy, paradoxical sensation of nasal blockage despite a wide nasal cavity, crusting, and fetid odour (ozaena). The patient here has watery discharge and congestion — the opposite of the dry atrophic picture.

answers.text: Acute viral rhinitis in the secretory phase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Acute viral rhinitis is self-limiting (7–10 days) and follows the classic stages of dry irritation, watery secretion, and mucopurulent discharge. A 5-year history of perennial symptoms cannot be explained by acute viral infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the clinical presentation and diagnostic criteria. The key discriminator from allergic rhinitis is negative allergy testing combined with non-immunological triggers.
Correct. Vasomotor rhinitis = perennial non-allergic nasal symptoms + physical/chemical triggers + negative allergy tests.
